items.title: Karl Berger interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, August 11, 2014
items.q: Karl co-founded the Creative Music Studio in Woodstock, New York with his wife, Ingrid Sertso.

ctx.x: I won’t be able to tell you. It’s how they hear the beat, or something the singer’s doing, or just the way —

Right. Just yesterday we had this experience. We were rehearsing a choir. Ingrid is conducting a choir at the Tibetan monastery. And we are working with actual mantras and with songs that are traditional — Tibetan traditional songs. And we invited five or six people into the choir who all said, “we are tone deaf and we can’t sing.” And all five of them at the end said, “can we come back next week?” Because there is no other experience other than getting involved in music. There is no other experience. It’s like…
Okay. This is I believe from one of your — oops I think I lost it. Let me find what I’m after here. You know some of your workshops are on YouTube. And I believe you are conducting this.

items.title: Ingrid Sertso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, August 11, 2014
items.q: met Karl and then we wanted to just build something up together. He played piano in the band I worked in... And we went there, Karl and me.

ctx.x: Okay. Well that music was pretty free to my ears. So if that was one of the first groundbreaking recordings, where does it go from there?

First of all, we have tourists coming up here that ask, roll your window down, “Is there any hippies around?” Just to answer what you asked before. Okay. Ornette invented the harmolodic approach to music and I think he helped us all to be confident in our need to really express ourselves freely. Where it goes from there, I wouldn’t know. For me, Ornette is the final, at the moment. Where it would go from there, I wouldn’t know. Because he is the most, that’s the most natural music to me. Ornette’s personal…

painting, music. Because my older brother was also — he brought me actually to my first jazz concert and he always painted with music, you know. He had records and it was his biggest inspiration. And then I got my own agent and I wanted to do jazz and I went into the whole standards thing. And then about three years later after I did it alone, I met Karl and then we wanted to just build something up together.
